unit-m34.title: Topic 3 · 3-4 Equivalent Decimals and Decimal Forms
unit-m34.source: enVision Math, Topic 3 textbook scan — Lessons 3-1 to 3-7 (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 3-4 covers equivalent decimals — zeros annexed after the last digit rename without changing — plus number names, standard form and expanded form for decimals, including the middle-zero cases where a zero is load-bearing.

why.text: Every comparison and every lined-up addition for the rest of the year quietly uses equivalence. The end-zero-versus-middle-zero distinction is also the first place this topic asks her to argue WHY, not just compute.

objectives.text: Write two decimals equivalent to a given decimal.
Convert between standard form, expanded form and number names for decimals.
Explain which zeros change a decimal's value and which do not.

parentNote.text: The Kai question is the heart of the lesson: end zeros are free, middle zeros re-seat everything. If she misses it, shading a hundredths grid for 7.63 vs 7.063 makes the difference visible in about thirty seconds.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz. The third card is the one that separates the free zeros from the load-bearing ones.

cards.def:
**Decimals that name the same amount.**
• 1.4 = 1.40 = 1.400.
• Four tenths, forty hundredths and four hundred thousandths are the same shaded amount.
cards.hint: Zeros glued to the END change nothing.

cards.def:
**Attaching zeros after the last decimal digit renames, never changes.**
• 0.6 → 0.60: six tenths become sixty hundredths.
• Useful for lining decimals up to compare or add.
cards.hint: Renaming into smaller pieces — the amount stays put.

cards.def:
**A zero between the point and the digits changes the value.**
• 7.63 and 7.630 are equal; 7.63 and 7.063 are not.
• Only zeros after the final digit are free.
cards.hint: End zeros are free; middle zeros are load-bearing.

cards.def:
**"And" marks the decimal point; the last seat names the part.**
• 4.068 → "four and sixty-eight thousandths".
• 9.20 → "nine and twenty hundredths".
cards.hint: Say "and" exactly where the point sits.

cards.def:
**Each digit times its seat, seats now including tenths, hundredths, thousandths.**
• 6.308 = (6 × 1) + (3 × 1/10) + (8 × 1/1,000).
• Empty seats simply do not appear.
cards.hint: The fractions 1/10, 1/100, 1/1,000 are the right-hand seats.

questions.hint: Only one option adds a zero at the END.
steps: Equivalent decimals differ only by zeros after the last digit.
5.30 attaches a zero at the end — same amount.
5.03 moves the 3 to a smaller seat — different amount.

ex.main: **5.30.** Five and three tenths equals five and thirty hundredths.
ex.tip: Say both out loud — "three tenths", "thirty hundredths" — and you can hear they match.

questions.q: How is "nine and twenty-four thousandths" written in standard form?
questions.hint: "Thousandths" fixes how many decimal places there are.
steps: "Nine and" gives the whole part: 9.
Twenty-four thousandths needs three decimal places.
024 fills them: 9.024.

ex.main: **9.024.** The zero holds the tenths seat that "twenty-four" leaves empty.
ex.tip: "And" is doing precise work in a number name — it is the decimal point.

questions.hint: Find the pair that differs only after its last nonzero digit.
steps: 2.60 just annexes a zero to 2.6 — equal.
2.06 puts the 6 in the hundredths seat — smaller.
2.66 adds six more hundredths — larger.

ex.main: **2.60 and 2.6.** Sixty hundredths is six tenths.
ex.tip: The zero's POSITION is the entire question, every time.

questions.q: What is the standard form of (6 × 1) + (3 × 1/10) + (8 × 1/1,000)?
questions.hint: One seat is missing from the sum — it still needs its zero.
steps: 6 × 1 = 6, whole part.
The hundredths seat has no term, so it gets a 0: 6.308.

ex.main: **6.308.** Expanded form skips empty seats; standard form writes their zeros.
ex.tip: The same silent-seat rule as whole numbers, now right of the point.

questions.q: Of the 1,000 raffle tickets printed for the school fair, 0.35 of them sold in the first hour. How many tickets is that?
steps: So 0.35 OF 1,000 tickets is 350 tickets.
Check: 0.35 is a bit more than a third of 1,000. ✓

ex.main: **350 tickets.** Annex a zero and the thousandths read straight off.
ex.tip: A decimal of a thousand is exactly why equivalent decimals earn their keep.

questions.q: Elena wrote 4.7 inches for a bug's length, but the real length is one-tenth of that. What is the correct measurement?
questions.hint: One-tenth slides every digit one seat right.
steps: One-tenth of a number moves each digit one seat right.

ex.main: **0.47 inches.** A misplaced decimal point is always a ×10 or ÷10 error.
ex.tip: When a measurement looks ten times too big, the point is the first suspect.

questions.q: Kai says 7.63 and 7.063 are equivalent because both just add a zero to 7.63. What should you tell him?
opts: Neither number is equivalent to anything
He is right — zeros never change a decimal
The zero in 7.063 sits between digits, so it changed the value
They would only be equal if the zero were removed from both
steps: 7.630 attaches the zero after the last digit — that one is equivalent.
7.063 slides the 6 and 3 into smaller seats.
7.063 is seven and sixty-three thousandths; 7.63 is seven and sixty-three hundredths.
Different seats, different number.

ex.main: **The zero moved the digits.** End zeros are free; a zero pushed between the point and the digits re-seats everything after it.
ex.tip: One rule, one exception-shaped trap — this is the whole lesson in a single question.

questions.q: Three friends shade hundredths grids. Priya shades half of one grid. Marco shades one full grid and one-tenth of another. What decimals show how much each shaded?
questions.hint: Half a grid is how many hundredths?
steps: Half of one hundredths grid is 50 squares: 0.50.
A full grid is 1, and one-tenth more is 0.10.

ex.main: **Priya 0.50, Marco 1.10.** Both amounts read straight off the grids.
ex.tip: 0.5 and 0.50 are the same — the grid just makes the hundredths version visible.

questions.q: Which is the number name for 12.406?
opts: Twelve and four hundred six thousandths
Twelve and four hundred six hundredths
One hundred twenty-four and six thousandths
questions.hint: The part after "and" is 406, and its last seat is thousandths.
steps: Whole part: twelve.
"And" for the point.
The decimal part is 406 ending in the thousandths seat.
So: twelve and four hundred six thousandths.

ex.main: **Twelve and four hundred six thousandths.** The middle zero is read inside 406, not skipped.
ex.tip: "Forty-six thousandths" would be 0.046 — the name has to carry the zero's work.

steps: The 8 is in the tenths seat: 8 × 1/10.
The 5 is in the hundredths seat: 5 × 1/100.

ex.main: **(8 × 1/10) + (5 × 1/100).** Each digit times exactly its seat.
ex.tip: Expanded form is the place-value chart written as arithmetic.
